newsitem.title: THAILAND: Burmese Karen rebels say Thais mediating for peace.
newsitem.headline: Burmese Karen rebels say Thais mediating for peace.

text.p: Ethnic Karen rebels fighting the Burmese military government said on Tuesday that Thai military officers had offered to act as mediators in an attempt to end the rebels' long fight for an independent homeland.
But a senior member of the Karen National Union (KNU) told Reuters that while the rebels welcomed the offer, they were sceptical about the real motive.
The KNU had met two Thai generals last week who had come to mediate between the rebels and the ruling Burmese State Law and Order Restoration Council (SLORC), he said.
"Any move to bring about peace is welcome but I am not so optimistic as it is unclear whether the SLORC urged the Thai army to be mediator or apply more pressure on us," he added.

Thai army commander in chief, General Chetta Tanajaro, was quoted by the Bangkok Post newspaper on Tuesday as saying the SLORC had urged him to mediate between it and minority rebels fighting Rangoon from near the Thai border.
A Thai military spokesmen could not confirm the statement attributed to General Chetta.
The KNU was formed in 1948 to fight for autonomy from Rangoon soon after Burma gained independence from Britain. It is regarded as the strongest rebel faction fighting the SLORC.
Dozens of smaller rebel factions have reached peace pacts with Burma's military rulers since they offered peace talks in the early 1990s.

About 100,000 Karen refugees, including women and children, who have fled fighting in Burma now live in sprawling camps near the Thai border under fear of reprisals by Burmese troops and those aligned with them.
Last week, top KNU officials met SLORC officials at the southeastern Burmese town of Moulmein for a fourth round of peace talks, but there was no breakthrough.
"The talks ended in stalemate because SLORC insisted that the KNU would have to unconditionally surrender and we cannot accept that," said a KNU official who asked not to be identified.
A smaller rebel group, the Karreni National Progress Party (KNPP), also said Thai generals had told them last week that Thailand would mediate at future peace talks.
"We welcome the move of the Thai army, provided that they have to guarantee that KNPP have (the) right to maintain its armed troops and self-rule in Kayah state," a Karreni official said.

KNPP guerrillas operating in northeastern Kayah state had concluded a ceasefire with Burmese troops in 1994. But the fighting resumed when the KNPP accused Rangoon of violating the ceasefire pact by sending thousands of troops to areas under its control.
